title: Compare Document Production Against Discovery Requests — Discovery Gap Analysis Memorandum

blind.coverage: Read in full: task.json (instructions plus all 46 criteria), rfps-first-set, meridian-rfp-responses, privilege-log (both sheets), production-index (all 332 rows parsed, plus the second 'Detailed Row-by-Row Content Pla' sheet), meet-confer-emails (all four messages), and scheduling-order. I searched complaint and answer-counterclaim with grep for the facts the criteria rely on (347/189 trucks, $5.1M, $31.4M/$22.7M EBITDA, Crestline, $215M, $14.3M, the 29-month term, breach notices, and board/management reports in Answer ¶223); I did not read them line by line. I checked production-index arithmetic with a script: 332 rows, contiguous Bates, 4,217 pages in total; rows coded to RFP 27 counted by row. I did not open the harness system_prompt or the judge prompt beyond what the task text describes. I fetched no primary legal texts this session, so every authority is marked unverified. I consulted no outside Harvey LAB commentary.

findings.title: RFP 27 counts ('9 of 14' Greystone; 'only 5' relate to damages) contradict the row-level production index
findings.explanation: The row-level index shows 8 Greystone documents (rows 309-316, MLC-003980 to MLC-004055), not 9. Only 13 rows are coded to RFP 27 alone; 15 are coded to it if you include rows 118 (16, 27) and 306 (25, 27). The '9 of 14' figure appears only in the index's leaked planning sheet (see O8). C-029's 'only 5 ... support is thin' is also undercut by rows 118 and 306, and by the RFP 25-coded counterclaim documents (rows 300-307: damages memo, damages spreadsheet, expert preliminary report). Judges do not see the documents, so they will treat '9 documents' and 'only 5' as the answer key. A memo that counts correctly (8 of 13, or 8 of 15) or notes the additional damages documents risks failing both criteria.

In C-029, drop 'only 5 ... thin' or acknowledge rows 118, 306 and 300-307.

findings.title: C-016 requires saying Meridian gave 'no explanation' for the dispatch-log gap, but its meet-and-confer emails give one
findings.explanation: Meridian's written RFP response offers no explanation. However, its September 2 and September 15, 2024 emails attribute the gap to a migration from RouteCast Pro to FleetBridge, with unmigrated and possibly unpreserved data. A competent memo would report that explanation and attack it as vague, a preservation or Rule 37(e) problem, and undercut by the absence of any objection in the written response. Under the plain wording, a judge may read such a memo as contradicting 'Meridian's response provides no explanation'. The criterion survives only if 'response' is read narrowly as the June 28 written response. It also rewards a memo that overlooks the later emails.

Meridian transitioned from its legacy fleet management system, RouteCast Pro, to its current platform, FleetBridge, in approximately Q4 2021. Certain data from the RouteCast Pro system was not migrated
Meridian underwent a transition to a new fleet management software system during late 2021, and some records from the transition period may not have been preserved in the ordinary course of business.

findings.suggested_fix: Change to: PASS if the memo notes that Meridian's written RFP response offered no objection or explanation for the gap, and that its later system-migration explanation is unsubstantiated or inadequate (or raises preservation concerns).

findings.title: C-006 asserts Crestline audited FY2020-2023; the record shows Crestline audits only for FY2019-2021
findings.explanation: No document says Crestline audited FY2022 or FY2023. The index lists Crestline-audited statements for FY2019, FY2020 and FY2021 only, and the complaint mentions only the FY2020 audit. The PASS condition therefore rewards stating a fact the record does not contain. The FAIL condition is lenient ('no argument ... that the audited financials likely exist'), so a memo that infers existence from the FY2019-2021 audit pattern, and from Meridian's promise to produce audited statements for 2019-2023, will probably pass. A literal judge could still fail a memo that declines to assert the FY2022-2023 audits.

findings.explanation: Row-level RFP 26 entries show Alderton corresponding with Denise Yamamoto (CEO) about service performance (rows 308 and 323). Cho's RFP 26 letters go to Pacific Corridor's accounts payable department about invoice disputes (rows 324-325). The 'Cho ... The underlying point, that the RFP 26 documents prove these custodians communicated directly with Pacific Corridor, is sound.

findings.title: C-032 says Meridian 'produced nothing' for RFP 16, but the index codes about 36 documents to RFP 16
findings.explanation: Meridian's written response to RFP 16 declines to produce. The production index, however, codes rows 88-123 (29 monthly invoices, an AR aging report, a revenue reconciliation, and general-ledger revenue extracts) to RFP 16. None of these are board presentations or management reports. A memo that says 'Meridian produced only invoices and GL extracts coded to RFP 16, with no board presentations or management analyses' is accurate but does not match 'produced nothing'. Most judges will focus on the counterclaim inconsistency and pass it, but the factual premise is inaccurate.

Based on the foregoing objections, Meridian does not produce documents in response to this Request.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'produced nothing' with 'refused production and produced no board presentations, management reports or internal financial analyses (documents coded to RFP 16 are only invoices and ledger extracts)'.

findings.title: C-033 requires the 'sword and shield' label and a 'waiver of objections' theory; the correct framing is Rule 26(b)(1) relevance
findings.explanation: The 'sword and shield' doctrine is at home in at-issue waiver of privilege. Meridian's objection to RFP 16 is relevance and proportionality, not privilege. Pleading a damages counterclaim does not 'waive' a relevance objection; it makes the financial materials relevant and proportional under Rule 26(b)(1), so the objection fails on the merits. Some courts use the phrase loosely in this setting, so the criterion is defensible. But it requires the label ('applying the sword and shield doctrine') and a stated waiver rule. A memo making the stronger, correct argument could fail a literal judge: the counterclaim puts Meridian's lost profits and financial performance at issue, and Answer ¶223 itself relies on 'management reports presented to ... board of directors'.

evidence.quote: applying the 'sword and shield' doctrine (i.e., a party that affirmatively pleads a damages claim waives objections to discovery of documents bearing on those claimed losses)
including account-level profit-and-loss statements, management reports presented to Meridian's senior leadership and board of directors

authorities.proposition: Discovery extends to nonprivileged matter relevant to any party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo argues that Meridian's $3.2M counterclaim puts its financial performance and lost profits at issue, so the RFP 16 materials are relevant and proportional and Meridian cannot rely on those same analyses while withholding them. Accept the 'sword and shield', 'at issue' or equivalent framing without requiring the label.

findings.title: C-025 calls the FMSA a '$14+ million' contract; $14.3M is Pacific Corridor's damages claim, not the contract value
findings.explanation: The record gives no contract value. $14.3M is Pacific Corridor's claimed compensatory damages (complaint ¶49, ¶211; scheduling order §1). The $215M figure is Meridian's FY2022 revenue, not its revenue when the contract was signed. The FAIL condition is lenient (no argument that board documents should exist), so most memos arguing that a five-year exclusive anchor contract would need board approval will pass. The PASS text, though, rewards mischaracterizing the damages figure as contract value, and a literal judge could expect it.

evidence.quote: for a $14+ million exclusive 5-year contract, board-level approval documentation should exist for a company of Meridian's size (~$215M annual revenue)
Pacific Corridor seeks compensatory damages of at least \$14.3 million, liquidated damages of \$1,407,000

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo argues that a five-year exclusive contract of this significance to a company of Meridian's size (about $215M revenue in FY2022) would ordinarily generate board approval records. Drop the '$14+ million contract' characterization.

findings.title: Supplied spreadsheets contain the task author's answer-key sheets, which label the planted issues; one contradicts the row data
findings.explanation: The privilege log's 'Full Entry Detail' sheet has group headers that announce the planted defects. The production index has a second 'Detailed Row-by-Row Content Pla[n]' sheet that states the gaps outright (e.g., zero RFP 8 documents, 'NO text messages', custodian gaps, '9 of 14 ... Greystone'). A real producing party would never serve these, and they hand solvers most of the answers, which weakens the task's ability to discriminate. The '9 of 14' figure in this sheet contradicts the index's own rows (8 Greystone documents; see O1). C-028 and C-029 track the leaked sheet rather than the data, so a solver who trusts the leak passes and one who counts the rows risks failing.

findings.title: Response restatements and index RFP codes do not match the served RFP numbering; other minor record inconsistencies
findings.explanation: Meridian's responses restate different requests under the served numbers. Response 2 and Response 3 misstate the served requests. Response 9 describes leases, but served RFP 9 is maintenance records. Response 10 describes maintenance, but served RFP 10 is the Fleet Capacity Report. Responses 12 and 13 are swapped. Response 18 describes board presentations, but served RFP 18 is lease obligations and ASC 842. The index codes follow neither numbering consistently: dispatch logs are coded '10, 20' rather than 19; invoices are coded 16; DOT audits 19; driver training 18; counterclaim emails 25. As a result, served RFP 18, which goes to the $3.6M in omitted lease liabilities, was effectively refused through a misdescribed response, and a correct memo must reconcile the numbering. This drives the C-032 premise problem (O5). Minor inconsistencies: the index sums to 332 rows, not the stated 312 documents (C-043's 'at least two of' avoids misgrading); the termination notice is dated August 22, 2023 in the complaint and RFP 26 but July 1, 2023 in index row 212; Alderton is CEO in the responses but COO in the index; the protective order is dated May 8, 2024 in the responses but July 10, 2024 in the emails.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound: most of its 46 criteria track real, well-planted gaps that the record supports. These include the missing RFP 8 and RFP 5 production, the FY2022-2023 audits, the 2022-only insurance policy, the dispatch-log gap, the custodian gap, the privilege-log problems (PRIV-12 to PRIV-18, PRIV-31 crime-fraud, PRIV-33 to PRIV-40 work product), the text-message gap, and the procedural facts (case number, court, October 1, 2024 deadline). The main risks are criteria whose embedded facts depart from the row-level record. Judges do not see the documents, so these embedded facts act as the answer key. C-028 and C-029 use the leaked '9 of 14' count, which the rows contradict. C-016 says Meridian gave 'no explanation' even though its meet-and-confer emails give one. C-006, C-018, C-025 and C-032 carry smaller factual overstatements that a precise memo could be penalized for. C-033 requires a doctrinal label and a waiver theory, where the stronger argument is Rule 26(b)(1) relevance. Separately, both spreadsheets contain the author's planning or answer-key sheets, and the RFP numbering is inconsistent across the requests, responses and index. Under all-pass scoring, O1 and O2 are the findings most likely to zero out an otherwise correct memo.

sol_verdicts.reason: The written Response 16 does refuse production. But index rows 88-123 are coded to RFP 16, and row 118 (a revenue reconciliation report for the Pacific Corridor account) arguably answers served RFP 16's clause covering Pacific Corridor-specific revenue analyses. So 'produced nothing' misstates the index. The FAIL trigger, however, is failing to identify the counterclaim inconsistency, so most accurate memos will still pass. The premise is inaccurate, but a misgrade is not certain.

I re-counted the index. 15 rows carry an RFP 27 code: rows 118 ('16, 27'), 306 ('25, 27') and 309-321. Of these, 8 concern Greystone (MLC-003980 to MLC-004055), not 9. Row 306 is itself the counterclaim damages spreadsheet, so 'only 5 relate' is false. The index has 332 numbered rows, while the summary says 312. C-043's 'at least two of' condition lets a memo pass using the correct page count and Bates range, so it carries only minor risk.

Every Crestline mention I checked supports audits for FY2019-2021 only (index rows 127-129; complaint on FY2020). Nothing in the record says Crestline audited FY2022 or FY2023. The PASS text therefore asserts an unsupported fact. The FAIL trigger is lenient ('no argument ... that the audited financials likely exist'), so a memo that infers the audits likely exist will usually pass. A literal judge could still fail it.

Meridian's RFP 16 objection rests on relevance and proportionality, not privilege. A damages counterclaim makes financial materials relevant; it does not categorically 'waive objections', because proportionality still applies. Courts do use 'sword and shield' loosely in this setting, so the core argument is reasonable. The risks are the required label and the overstated waiver parenthetical, which could fail a memo that makes the correct Rule 26(b)(1) at-issue argument without them.

C-018: the index shows Alderton corresponding with the CEO (row 308), while Cho's RFP 26 letters went to accounts payable about invoices (rows 324-325). 'Cho ... CEO ... service failures' comes from plaintiff counsel's letter, and 'proving ... must exist' overstates. C-025: $14.3M is the damages claim, not the contract value. C-027: accurate. The RFP 23 objection targets the 'any employee' scope, and Meridian promised to produce custodian texts, so calling their total absence implausible is reasonable advocacy.

Response 15 asserts only a general overbreadth objection and promises audited and unaudited statements for 2019-2023. No privilege-log entry covers FY2022-2023 audits. The criterion speaks of a privilege or specific objection 'for the FY2022 and FY2023 audited financial statements', and none exists. A memo that mentions the general objection still satisfies it.

final.changes_from_blind: I downgraded blind O2 (C-016) from problematic to arguable. The criterion is literally true of Meridian's written RFP 19 response, and a memo discussing the migration explanation will usually also note that silence, so it misgrades only some memos. I split blind O8: the answer-key leak is now a document defect with no criteria attached (O8). I no longer list C-008, C-022, C-024, C-026 or C-030 as affected, because those criteria are themselves sound, and the count problem stays in O1 (C-028, C-029). I narrowed blind O9 to C-043 and dropped C-032 and C-046: served and restated RFP 16 match in substance, and C-046's categories follow the served numbering. I added Sol's point that row 118 (a Pacific Corridor revenue reconciliation) is arguably responsive to served RFP 16, which strengthens O5, and that row 118 bears on C-029. After checking, I rejected Sol's C-007 and C-027 findings as not defects. I held C-006, C-032 and C-033 at arguable, where Sol has them as confirmed, because each criterion's lenient FAIL trigger limits the misgrade risk. I could not verify the text of Rule 26: WebFetch failed because a spend limit was reached.
final.overall: The rubric mostly tracks real, well-planted gaps that the record supports: RFP 5 and RFP 8, the dispatch-log gap, the custodian gap, the privilege-log groups, texts, and the procedural facts. The clearest defect is in C-028 and C-029, which take the RFP 27 counts ('9 of 14' Greystone, 'only 5' relevant) from the leaked planning sheet. The index rows contradict them: 8 Greystone documents, 15 coded rows, and the counterclaim damages spreadsheet (row 306) among the relevant ones. Under all-pass scoring, those two criteria alone can zero out an accurate memo. Several other criteria embed smaller factual overstatements that a precise memo could be penalized for: C-006, C-016, C-018, C-025 and C-032.
